criterion_notes.c1: No. Although the chapter includes a section on the Kibera Integrated Water Sanitation and Waste Management Project (K-WATSAN) and reproduces baseline survey counts naming sanitation (n = 135) and water (n = 2) among negative attributes of living in Kibera, it does not examine household or community access to water or sanitation services. Instead, K-WATSAN is examined strictly as a community-mobilization and trust-building catalyst ('entry point') for an affordable housing slum-upgrading programme (Soweto East Phase 1 / Canaan Estate).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, the chapter DOES examine institutional and local governance factors—specifically a multi-stakeholder partnership among the Kenyan Government (KENSUP), UN-Habitat, the NGO Maji na Ufanisi, and the democratically elected Settlement Executive Committee (SEC)—so it passes Criterion 2 on its literal broad wording (though plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because the study still fails Criteria 1 and 4 for lack of water/sanitation service-access analysis and outcomes). Under the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is 'no': for the water and sanitation component (K-WATSAN), the chapter describes only generic participatory project delivery, community mobilization, awareness creation, youth clean-ups, and construction employment duty rosters rather than any rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation service access. Meanwhile, the only rule-type eligibility, pricing, and litigation mechanisms analysed (a 10% housing-cooperative savings deposit, public balloting, negotiated 20-year unit purchase prices, and a civil court challenge by structure owners delaying site clearance) govern housing unit acquisition and land clearance for housing, not water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Although the chapter lacks a formal methodology section, it presents empirical perceptions distributions from a Phase 1 field survey in Kibera (N = 407 and N = 424 respondents, reproduced from Meredith and MacDonald 2014) alongside primary qualitative case-study observations from site visits and discussions with Phase 1 project participants and Phase 2 community leaders.
criterion_notes.c4: No. No outcome measuring water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is reported. Section 15.5 ('The Project and the Outcome') reports only community trust/support and the completion and allocation of 822 affordable housing units in Canaan Estate (plus initiation of Phase 2 housing clearance).
criterion_notes.c5: No. While the settlement population (residents of Soweto East Zone A, Kibera, Nairobi) and descriptive case-study design are identifiable, neither a rule-type exposure governing water or sanitation access nor any water or sanitation service-access outcome can be identified because the eligibility rules and outcomes analysed pertain to housing allocation and community engagement.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. Full text is in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: The project therefore used water and sanitation as the entry point to the slum upgrading in Soweto East, Zone A, and the Kibera Integrated Water Sanitation and Waste Management Project (K-WATSAN) was initiated.
The community involvement in planning, management and execution of the water and sanitation projects gave them a sense of self-esteem and recognition.

The selection of families was done openly and transparently, through a balloting process in the National Stadium witnessed by the Cabinet Minister for Housing. Those eligible for the draw had savings, based on their participation in community cooperatives initiated and supported by the community development team.

To address these we draw upon data from a field survey undertaken during Phase 1 (Meredith and Macdonald, 2014), which investigated factors seen as positive aspects of the community and factors seen as challenges.
Phase 1 of the Soweto East Project succeeded largely because K-WATSAN and KENSUP met their target of winning community support.

raw_response.exposure: Participatory slum-upgrading partnership and community mobilization mechanisms involving the Government of Kenya (KENSUP), UN-Habitat, NGO Maji na Ufanisi, and an elected Settlement Executive Committee (SEC), plus housing cooperative savings (10% deposit), negotiated unit payment rates, and balloting for housing unit allocation
raw_response.outcome: Community trust, mobilization, and support for slum upgrading, and completion and allocation of 822 affordable housing units in Canaan Estate (plus initiation of Phase 2 housing clearance); no water or sanitation service access outcomes reported
raw_response.population_and_sample: Informal settlement residents and community stakeholders in Soweto East (Zone A), Kibera, Nairobi, Kenya (reprinted Phase 1 survey charts report N = 407 and N = 424 respondents of known age; qualitative observations from Phase 1 participants and Phase 2 community leaders; 822 families allocated housing units in Canaan Estate)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded (E07 Wrong service; also fails Criterion 2 exposure and Criterion 4 outcome for water/sanitation). Although this book chapter discusses the Kibera Integrated Water Sanitation and Waste Management Project (K-WATSAN) and reproduces 2014 survey counts showing sanitation as a perceived problem in Kibera, K-WATSAN is analysed solely as a participatory community-mobilization and trust-building 'entry point' for an affordable housing upgrading programme (KENSUP Soweto East Phase 1). First, the substantive service access/allocation examined is housing (822 housing units in Canaan Estate), not household or community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no, E07). Second, under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification of Criterion 2, the water and sanitation component involves only generic participatory project delivery, outreach, clean-ups, and construction employment rosters rather than a rule-type mechanism governing water or sanitation access, while the 10% cooperative deposit, negotiated unit prices, and balloting rules govern housing acquisition (c2 = no). Third, no water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcome is reported (c4 = no); consequently, even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study would still be excluded.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative descriptive case study of Phase 1 of the KENSUP Soweto East slum upgrading project, drawing on site visits, discussions with community leaders and Phase 1 participants, and reprinted descriptive perceptions data from an earlier Phase 1 field survey
